title: Triangles
weightage: 2–4 questions (the backbone of CAT Geometry; feeds circles, mensuration & coordinate geometry)
intro: Triangles are the load-bearing wall of CAT Geometry. Almost every other geometry result — properties of circles, polygons, coordinate geometry, even mensuration of 3-D solids — is ultimately built on a triangle drawn inside the figure, so the student who is fluent here clears the whole domain faster. CAT does not ask you to recite the angle-sum property; it hides a 30-60-90 triangle inside a hexagon, or asks for a ratio of areas that only the similarity rule unlocks. This chapter develops the four ideas the exam actually tests: congruence (proving two triangles are identical so a length or angle transfers), similarity and the (side ratio)² area rule that is the single highest-yield shortcut in the section, the Pythagoras theorem with its recurring triples, and the four classical centres — centroid, incentre, circumcentre and orthocentre — together with the two area links R = abc/(4·Area) and Area = r·s. Each topic comes with worked CAT-style examples, the fastest method, and the specific traps that cost careless aspirants a clean two marks.

topics.name: Congruence
topics.details: Two triangles are congruent when they are identical in shape AND size — every pair of corresponding sides and angles matches. In CAT you almost never "prove" congruence formally; instead you use it as a tool to transfer a known length or angle from one triangle to an unknown one in the same figure. There are exactly four valid tests: SSS (all three sides equal), SAS (two sides and the INCLUDED angle), ASA (two angles and the included side) — and its cousin AAS — and RHS (right angle, hypotenuse and one side) for right triangles. The single most common trap is SSA, sometimes called the "ambiguous case": two sides and a non-included angle do NOT guarantee congruence. Note also that AAA only proves similarity, never congruence, because the triangles can scale. Once congruence is established, corresponding parts (CPCT) are equal, which is usually the fact the question secretly needs.

solved.problem: In triangle ABC, AB = AC and AD is the median to BC. State the test that proves triangle ABD ≅ triangle ACD and the consequence.
solved.solution: AB = AC (given), BD = DC (median), AD = AD (common) ⇒ SSS. Hence by CPCT angle ADB = angle ADC, and as they are a linear pair each is 90°, so the median to the base of an isosceles triangle is also the altitude.

solved.problem: Two triangles have sides 6, 8 and included angle 50°, and 6, 8 with included angle 50°. Are they congruent? By which test?
solved.solution: Two sides and the angle BETWEEN them are equal, so SAS applies ⇒ the triangles are congruent.

solved.problem: A triangle has sides 7 and 9 with a 40° angle opposite the side of length 7. Is a triangle with the same data necessarily congruent to it?
solved.solution: The 40° is NOT between the two sides — this is the SSA / ambiguous case. Two non-congruent triangles can fit the data, so congruence is NOT guaranteed.

solved.problem: Right triangles PQR and XYZ have right angles at Q and Y, hypotenuses PR = XZ = 13 and legs PQ = XY = 5. Are they congruent, and what is the third side?
solved.solution: Right angle + equal hypotenuse + equal one side ⇒ RHS, so the triangles are congruent. The remaining leg = √(13² − 5²) = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12.

unsolved.problem: Which single test proves congruence of two triangles given all three pairs of sides equal?
Triangles with (5, 7, 60° included) and (5, 7, 60° included): congruent? Name the test.
hints: The angle is between the two sides.

unsolved.problem: Does AAA (all three angles equal) prove two triangles congruent?
hints: A small and a large copy share angles.

unsolved.problem: In a right triangle, hypotenuse 25 and one leg 7. The other leg?
Two triangles share two equal sides and a non-included equal angle. Is congruence guaranteed?
unsolved.answer: No — SSA does not guarantee congruence

topics.name: Similarity & Area Ratios
topics.details: Similar triangles have the same shape but possibly different size: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in a fixed ratio k. The fastest test in CAT is AA — if two angles match, the third must too, so the triangles are similar. The result the exam loves is the area rule: if the sides are in ratio k (say 3 : 5), the areas are in ratio k² (9 : 25). Perimeters, medians, altitudes, inradii and circumradii all scale linearly with k, but areas scale with k². A second high-yield tool is the Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales): a line parallel to one side of a triangle cuts the other two sides in the same ratio, creating a smaller similar triangle. Whenever you see parallel lines, a midpoint, or two triangles sharing an angle inside a figure, reach for similarity first — it converts an awkward length into a clean proportion in one line.

solved.problem: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 3 : 4. Find the ratio of their areas.
In triangle ABC, DE ∥ BC with D on AB and E on AC. If AD = 4, DB = 6, AE = 5, find EC.
The areas of two similar triangles are 50 cm² and 98 cm². If a side of the smaller is 10 cm, find the corresponding side of the larger.
A vertical pole 6 m tall casts a 4 m shadow. A nearby tower casts a 30 m shadow at the same time. Find the tower’s height.
solved.solution: Sun’s rays give similar right triangles, so height/shadow is constant: 6/4 = h/30 ⇒ h = 30 × 6/4 = 45 m.

unsolved.problem: Similar triangles have sides in ratio 2 : 5. Ratio of areas?
Areas of two similar triangles are 16 : 49. Ratio of corresponding sides?
hints: Sides scale as the square root of areas.

unsolved.problem: DE ∥ BC; AD = 3, DB = 5, AE = 6. Find EC.
A smaller similar triangle has half the perimeter of a larger one. What fraction is its area?
Two similar triangles have areas 45 and 80. The smaller has a median of 9. Find the larger triangle’s corresponding median.

topics.name: Pythagoras
topics.details: In a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. The fastest CAT students never crunch the algebra — they recognise the standard Pythagorean triples on sight: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, and 9-40-41, together with every multiple (6-8-10, 9-12-15, 10-24-26, and so on). Spotting that 39 and 52 are 3 × 13 and 4 × 13 instantly gives a hypotenuse of 65. The converse is equally useful: if a² + b² = c² the triangle is right-angled, while a² + b² > c² makes it acute and a² + b² < c² obtuse, which lets you classify a triangle from its sides alone. Two special right triangles recur constantly: the 45-45-90 with sides in ratio 1 : 1 : √2, and the 30-60-90 with sides in ratio 1 : √3 : 2 — memorise both, because hexagons, equilateral triangles and squares cut along a diagonal all produce them.

solved.problem: A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse without long multiplication.
solved.solution: 9-12-15 is the 3-4-5 triple scaled by 3, so the hypotenuse is 15. (Check: 81 + 144 = 225 = 15².)

solved.problem: The diagonal of a square is 10√2 cm. Find the side and the area.
solved.solution: Diagonal = side × √2 ⇒ side = 10√2/√2 = 10 cm. Area = 10² = 100 cm².

solved.problem: A 30-60-90 triangle has its shortest side 7. Find the other two sides.
solved.solution: Ratio 1 : √3 : 2 ⇒ sides are 7, 7√3 and 14 (the side opposite 60° is 7√3, the hypotenuse 14).

solved.problem: Are the sides 7, 8, 12 a right, acute or obtuse triangle?
solved.solution: Compare 7² + 8² = 49 + 64 = 113 with 12² = 144. Since 113 < 144, the triangle is obtuse.

unsolved.problem: Legs 8 and 15. Hypotenuse?
A right triangle has hypotenuse 26 and one leg 10. Other leg?
Diagonal of a square of side 8?
In a 45-45-90 triangle the hypotenuse is 14. Each leg?
Classify the triangle with sides 6, 8, 9.

topics.name: Centres of a Triangle
topics.details: Four classical points govern a triangle. The CENTROID (G) is where the three medians meet; it divides every median in a 2 : 1 ratio from the vertex and is the triangle’s centre of mass. The INCENTRE (I) is where the angle bisectors meet — the centre of the inscribed circle of radius r, and it gives the clean area link Area = r × s, where s is the semi-perimeter. The CIRCUMCENTRE (O) is where the perpendicular bisectors of the sides meet — the centre of the circle through all three vertices, of radius R = abc/(4·Area); for a right triangle O sits at the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so R = hypotenuse/2. The ORTHOCENTRE (H) is where the three altitudes meet. In any triangle G, O and H are collinear on the Euler line with HG : GO = 2 : 1. For an equilateral triangle all four centres coincide and R = 2r. CAT favours the two area relations and the right-triangle circumradius shortcut.

solved.problem: A median of a triangle is 18 cm long. How far is the centroid from the vertex and from the midpoint of the opposite side?
solved.solution: The centroid divides the median 2 : 1 from the vertex. Vertex side = (2/3) × 18 = 12 cm; midpoint side = (1/3) × 18 = 6 cm.

solved.problem: A triangle has sides 13, 14, 15. Find its inradius.
A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. Find its circumradius.
solved.solution: Hypotenuse = √(36+64) = 10. In a right triangle the circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse, so R = 10/2 = 5.

solved.problem: For the 13-14-15 triangle (Area 84), find the circumradius R.

unsolved.problem: A median is 21 cm. Distance from the centroid to the vertex?
hints: Centroid splits the median 2 : 1 from the vertex.

unsolved.problem: A triangle has Area 30 and semi-perimeter 10. Inradius?
A right triangle has hypotenuse 26. Circumradius?
hints: Circumcentre is the midpoint of the hypotenuse.

unsolved.problem: An equilateral triangle has side 6. Inradius?
In a triangle, HG : GO on the Euler line is 2 : 1. If GO = 4, find HO.

shortcuts: Spot Pythagorean triples on sight — 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25, 9-40-41 and all multiples — to skip square-root work.
For similar triangles: sides, perimeters, medians and radii scale by k; areas scale by k². Square the side ratio for areas.
Any line parallel to a side (Thales/BPT) instantly splits the other two sides in equal ratio — use it whenever you see ∥ marks.
Right-triangle circumradius is just half the hypotenuse; no need for R = abc/(4·Area).
Memorise the two special triangles: 45-45-90 → 1 : 1 : √2 and 30-60-90 → 1 : √3 : 2.
Use Area = r·s to get the inradius and R = abc/(4·Area) for the circumradius once Heron’s area is known.
mistakes: Treating SSA or AAA as a congruence test — SSA is ambiguous and AAA gives similarity only.
Using the side ratio for the area of similar triangles instead of its square (k vs k²).
Mislabelling the hypotenuse — Pythagoras only works with c as the side opposite the right angle.
Splitting the median in the wrong direction — the 2 : 1 part is from the VERTEX, not from the midpoint.
Forgetting the triangle inequality, so an impossible triangle (e.g. sides 2, 3, 6) is accepted.
pyq: CAT and XAT favour triangles that hide inside other figures rather than stand alone: a 30-60-90 inside a regular hexagon, similar triangles formed by a chord and a tangent, or an area split by a cevian. Recurring patterns are the (side ratio)² area question, Basic Proportionality with a parallel line, right-triangle setups solved by recognising a triple, and inradius/circumradius links via Heron’s area. Pure-memory questions are rare; the marks go to students who recognise the embedded similar pair or the standard triple instantly. Difficulty is Moderate–Hard, and accuracy here lifts the whole Geometry block.

summary: Triangles anchor CAT Geometry. Prove identical triangles with SSS, SAS, ASA/AAS or RHS — never SSA or AAA. Similar triangles (AA test) scale lengths by k and areas by k², and a parallel line (BPT) splits the other two sides equally. Pythagoras gives a² + b² = c²; recognise the triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17, 7-24-25 and the special 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles. Four centres matter: centroid (median split 2 : 1 from the vertex), incentre (Area = r·s), circumcentre (R = abc/(4·Area), half the hypotenuse in a right triangle) and orthocentre (G, O, H collinear on the Euler line, HG : GO = 2 : 1).
